例句

  • Strong relationships with family and friends help us deal with stress and anxiety.（和家人朋友关系好，能帮我们应对压力和焦虑。）
  • Loneliness is now seen as a serious health factor, just like smoking.（孤独现在被看作一个严重的健康因素，跟吸烟一样。）
  • Psychologists have discovered that our early bonds with parents affect our adult relationships.（心理学家发现，我们小时候跟父母的联系会影响成年后的感情关系。）
  • Moving to a new country can be an intense emotional experience, but most people survive it and become more confident.（移居新国家可能是一段情绪很强烈的经历，但大多数人都能挺过来，变得更自信。）

过关标准：遮住中文看英文，能说出 22 个以上的意思，再挑 5 个自己造句（最好跟家人朋友、情绪压力有关，口语 Part 1 和 Part 3 常考）。

BBC 6 Minute English：Why does heartbreak hurt so much?（10 月 1 日）。音频和原文都已经放在页面里，不用打开 BBC 网站。

  1. 先把上面的听前生词过一遍。听不太懂的话，可以先点开下面的原文读懂再听。
  2. 第一遍不看文字，只听大意，回答开头的问题：上世纪 50 年代心理学家发现，小时候跟父母的联系会影响成年后的恋爱关系，这个理论叫什么？a) contraction theory b) attachment theory c) superstition theory
  3. 第二遍点开下面的原文精听，听不出的地方暂停、倒回去并标出来。两位专家（Dr Lucy Brown 和 Professor Zoe Donaldson）语速快一点，可以多听几遍。
  4. 第三遍挑 Neil 讲 2013 年那个研究的一段（"Well, being in love doesn't just change..."）跟读，模仿语调和连读。
  5. 记住 6 个表达：heartbreak（心碎）、addicted to（对…上瘾）、oriented / orientated towards（以…为中心）、social bonds（社会纽带，亲密关系）、longevity（寿命）、ex（前任）。
点开看原文（难词带中文，点虚线词显示）

Neil：Hi Georgie.

Georgie：Hi Neil.

Neil：Now, I want you to think back to回想 the last time you had your heart broken心碎. How did it feel?

Georgie：It was a couple of几个，两三个 years ago. And I just remember a really intense, sad emotion. But it also sometimes feels like a physical pain in your stomach, doesn't it?

Neil：It does. It's like real pain, isn't it? And today, in 6 Minute English, we're talking about heartbreak心碎. Now, heartbreak心碎 is the feeling of sadness we get when we lose someone we love. And that pain you feel, it's not just imaginary想象中的，虚构的. In this podcast, we'll be understanding how our brains change when we fall in love坠入爱河 and asking the question, why does heartbreak心碎 hurt so much?

Georgie：And as usual, we'll be learning some useful new vocabulary. You can find the full list and the definitions at bbclearningenglish.com.

Neil：Georgie, we're going to start with a quiz question. Are you ready?

Georgie：I am very ready.

Neil：So, in the 1950s, psychologists心理学家 noticed a link between children's early bonds with their parents and their romantic恋爱的；浪漫的 relationships as adults, but what is this theory called? Is it:

a) contraction收缩；缩略 theory,

b) attachment依恋；依附 theory, or

c) superstition迷信 theory?

Georgie：I think it's b) attachment依恋；依附 theory.

Neil：OK. Well, we will find out弄清楚，得知 at the end of the programme.

Georgie：What's going on in our brains when we fall in love坠入爱河?

Neil：Well, scientists have scanned扫描 people's brains while they're looking at a photo of their romantic恋爱的；浪漫的 partner. And they found that looking at someone you're in love with activates激活，使活跃 a part of the brain that also reminds us to eat and drink.

Georgie：And do scientists know why being in love impacts our brain in this way?

Neil：So, it's all about survival生存. Our brains have evolved进化 to be this way. Dr Lucy Brown explains more to the BBC World Service.

Dr Lucy Brown：This is a survival生存 system. Nature gave us these systems to be addicted上瘾的 to each other – for reproduction繁殖，生育, for protection. You're oriented使朝向；以…为中心（oriented） completely toward the other person. It's like hunger or thirst口渴.

Georgie：Lucy says our brains make us addicted上瘾的 to our romantic恋爱的；浪漫的 partners. If you're addicted上瘾的 to something, you want more of it. You can literally be addicted上瘾的 to things like drugs or alcohol, but we also use it metaphorically比喻地 to talk about things we love.

Neil：She says that romantic恋爱的；浪漫的 partners are oriented使朝向；以…为中心（oriented） to each other, which in British English we say orientated使朝向；以…为中心（oriented）, and it means they are pointed towards each other. They think of each other before other people.

Georgie：Neil, is there anything else scientists have discovered from scanning扫描 the brains of people in love?

Neil：Well, being in love doesn't just change the way we think. It changes our whole identity身份；自我认同. A 2013 study showed us more about this. People were shown statements about themselves – for example, Neil is kind – and the part of the brain we use to think about ourselves lit up亮起来（大脑区域变活跃）. When showing the same statements about their partner, the same part of the brain was active – not the part of the brain we generally use to think about others.

Georgie：So, Neil, are all of these brain changes that come with being in love actually good for us?

Neil：Well, studies suggest that good social connections社会联系 help manage stress and support our immune system免疫系统. Professor Zoe Donaldson explained more to the BBC World Service.

Professor Zoe Donaldson：Having really strong social bonds社会纽带，亲密关系 increases your likelihood可能性 that you'll survive from just about anything几乎任何事, whether that be cancer, depression抑郁症, etc. And it overall is the number one predictor预测指标 of longevity寿命；长寿. So, if you are lonely and you don't have bonds, then your mortality死亡率 risk goes up in a way that's equivalent相当的，等同的 to being obese肥胖的 or smoking.

Georgie：So, having strong social bonds社会纽带，亲密关系 or close relationships with other people makes you more likely to survive disease, according to Zoe.

Neil：Yes, it's an important factor in our longevity寿命；长寿, which means how long we live. In fact, Zoe says, being lonely and not having good social bonds社会纽带，亲密关系 increases your mortality死亡率 risk, your risk of dying, by as much as being obese肥胖的 or smoking.

Georgie：OK. So, what happens when these bonds are broken, when we experience heartbreak心碎?

Neil：Well, scientists have been looking at this by asking people to look at photos of their exes前任们, their former partners前任伴侣, and scanning扫描 their brains. They found that heartbreak心碎 activates激活，使活跃 parts of the brain we use when we're in danger or in pain. Professor Zoe Donaldson explains more.

Professor Zoe Donaldson：It's literal pain in your brain. So, if you look at the parts of the brain that light up亮起来（大脑区域变活跃）, they overlap重叠 with the same brain regions大脑区域 that are activated激活，使活跃 when you feel visceral内脏的；发自身体深处的 pain – when you feel actual, you know... like you get a burn, or you break a... you break a bone.

Neil：OK. So, now it's time for the answer to the quiz question I asked you. It was about a theory developed by psychologists心理学家 in the 1950s, which says that children's early relationships with their parents impact their relationships as adults. What's the name of the theory?

Georgie：I was quite confident about this, wasn't I, Neil? I said attachment依恋；依附 theory.

Neil：Well, you had a reason to be confident because you are correct.

Georgie：Yay! OK. Let's recap回顾；总结 the vocabulary we learnt in this programme, starting with heartbreak心碎, which is the feeling you experience after you lose someone you love.

Neil：If you're addicted上瘾的 to someone or something, you want more of it all the time.

Georgie：Oriented使朝向；以…为中心（oriented） or orientated使朝向；以…为中心（oriented） towards is used metaphorically比喻地 to mean that someone or something is your main focus.

Neil：Social bonds社会纽带，亲密关系 are the close relationships we have with family, friends and romantic恋爱的；浪漫的 partners.

Georgie：Longevity寿命；长寿 means how long you'll live.

Neil：And an ex is a past romantic恋爱的；浪漫的 partner that you are no longer in a relationship with.

Georgie：Once again, our six minutes are up, but you can test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website. Go to bbclearningenglish.com.

Neil：Thanks for joining us and goodbye.

Georgie：Goodbye.

过关标准：不看原文能用中文说出这集讲了什么（恋爱时大脑怎么变化，亲密关系为什么对健康重要，心碎为什么真的会痛），6 个表达都知道意思，Neil 那段能流利读下来。

小练习

  1. Many teenagers are ______ ______ their phones.（两个词，对手机上瘾）
  2. Eating well and staying active can improve your ______.（寿命）
  3. She met her ______ at a party and it was really awkward.（前任）
  4. Strong ______ ______ protect us from stress and illness.（两个词，社会纽带）
  5. After the breakup, he suffered from ______ for months.（心碎）
点开看答案

开头那题选 b，attachment theory（依恋理论）。填空：1. addicted to 2. longevity 3. ex 4. social bonds 5. heartbreak
